searchText: > the same with INVALID opcode The invalid opcode was supposed to be retroactively applied, because it was an opcode which was never allocated and we agreed *not to allocate it* for any other purposes, e.g. it applies from genesis. https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1803 proposes to rename it to ABORT though, to more clearly articulate its meaning. The current "the INVALID opcode, not that other invalid opcode" is a bit messy 🙂 We found a nice way of retroactively apply many opcodes, if we are allowed to form a list of transactions that are the exceptions. For these transaction, we simply burn all given gas. For all others, we can pretend that the opcodes existed from the beginning I think this can be applied to all opcodes except REVERT for REVERT the exception list will be way too long why is this? because there were a lot of transactions using code that had unused REVERT code in it? did you look at mainnet, or just one of the testnets? It was checked only on testnet. I suspect that in mainnet, there won't be many such exceptions even for REVERT who wanted to waste real money on these? 🙂 A good point. <@329594653097721856> I know that it'll take a lot of time, but it worth it to check in mainnet. You also can stop the check immediately if it's too much exceptions. It won't take a lot of time, if you are using our implementation 😉 Golang is not that bad, Artem :)

excerpts.author: axic3354
excerpts.content:
>  the same with INVALID opcode

The invalid opcode was supposed to be retroactively applied, because it was an opcode which was never allocated and we agreed *not to allocate it* for any other purposes, e.g. it applies from genesis.

excerpts.author: axic3354
excerpts.content: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1803 proposes to rename it to ABORT though, to more clearly articulate its meaning. The current "the INVALID opcode, not that other invalid opcode" is a bit messy 🙂
